content: Water supply refers to the process of providing water, either through self-provision or by third parties, to various users. This includes water of different qualities for domestic, industrial, and agricultural purposes. Currently, the focus is on public water supply, but industrial self-supply and irrigation are also significant aspects. Globally, approximately 5 billion people (54% of the population) have access to piped water through household connections, while 3 billion (20%) rely on alternative safe water sources such as standpipes, water kiosks, protected springs, and wells. However, over 1 billion people (16%) lack access to safe water, forcing them to use unprotected sources like wells, springs, canals, lakes, or rivers. Water and Public Health Adequate water quantity and quality are critical for public health and hygiene. Waterborne diseases are a leading cause of illness and death in lowand middle-income countries. For instance, around 900 million people suffer from water-related diarrheal diseases annually, with approximately 2 million deaths. Diarrhea and intestinal worm infestations account for at least 17% of the total disease burden in many developing nations. Common waterborne diseases include diarrhea, typhoid, and cholera. Trachoma, an infectious eye disease leading to blindness, is also linked to poor water supply, inadequate sanitation, and improper human waste management. In cases of suspected or actual water contamination, authorities may issue a boil water advisory to mitigate health risks. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends a minimum of 20 liters of water per person per day for basic access, with 100 liters per person per day considered optimal for low health risks. Technical Overview of Water Supply Water supply systems source water from groundwater (aquifers), surface water (lakes and rivers), conservation efforts, and desalination of seawater. The water is typically purified, disinfected (commonly through chlorination or ultraviolet light), and sometimes fluoridated. Treated water is then distributed via gravity or pumped to reservoirs, such as elevated water towers or ground-level storage facilities. After use, wastewater is discharged into sewer systems, treated at wastewater treatment plants, and either released into natural water bodies or reused for landscaping, irrigation, or industrial purposes. Despite access to piped water, many people, especially in developing countries, receive poor-quality services. Service quality is assessed based on continuity, water quality, pressure, and responsiveness to customer complaints. Continuity of supply is often taken for granted in developed countries but remains a significant issue in developing nations, where water may only be available for a few hours daily or weekly. Approximately half of the population in developing countries experiences intermittent water supply. Water Quality and Pressure Drinking water quality encompasses microbiological and physicochemical parameters. Public water systems must ensure disinfection, often through chlorination or ultraviolet light, and may require additional treatment, especially for surface water sources. Water pressure varies across distribution systems. High-pressure mains may require pressure reducers at entry points to buildings, while poorly managed systems may experience excessively low or high pressures, leading to inadequate flow or damage to plumbing fixtures. Urban water systems typically maintain pressure through pressurized tanks, elevated towers, or pumping stations. In the UK, urban water pressure averages 4-5 bars, though some areas may exceed 8 bars. Variations in pressure can also result from hydrostatic pressure differences due to elevation changes. Comparing Water and Sanitation Service Providers Benchmarking the performance of water and sanitation utilities is essential due to the natural monopoly of the sector, which limits direct competition. Performance comparisons simulate competition, set realistic improvement targets, and encourage lagging utilities to catch up with best practices. The International Benchmarking Network for Water and Sanitation Utilities provides data for such assessments. Institutional Responsibility and Governance Water supply responsibilities are divided between policy/regulation and service provision. Policies and regulations are typically defined by government ministries or agencies, such as the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) in the United States. In some countries, regulatory functions are assigned to independent agencies to protect consumers and improve efficiency. These agencies may approve tariff increases, manage sector information systems, and resolve consumer complaints. However, their autonomy varies, and in many countries, they face challenges in exercising independence. Service Provision Water supply providers differ in geographical coverage, sectoral responsibilities, ownership structures, and governance arrangements. Some utilities serve single cities, while others operate regionally or nationally. In rural areas, community-based organizations often manage water services. Utilities may focus solely on water supply or also handle sewerage, wastewater treatment, electricity distribution, and solid waste collection. Integrated utilities, such as those in Medellín, Colombia, and Frankfurt, Germany, offer multiple services, enabling benefits like common billing and cross-subsidization. Tariffs and Metering Most water providers charge tariffs to recover costs, but few achieve full cost recovery. Tariffs vary widely, with higher rates in developed countries. In developing nations, tariffs often fail to cover costs, and subsidies are common. Metering is considered best practice, promoting water conservation, delaying costly system expansions, and enabling fair cost allocation. Metering methods range from manual readings to advanced automatic meter reading (AMR) systems. Costs and Financing Water supply costs are predominantly fixed, including capital and personnel expenses, with variable costs like energy and chemicals playing a smaller role. In developed countries, urban water supply costs range from $1-2 per cubic meter, with similar costs for sanitation. These costs are partially billed to consumers, with subsidies covering the remainder. Financing mechanisms include internally generated revenues, commercial bank loans, international financial institution credits, and bonds. Historical Context Throughout history, societies have developed systems to improve water access and convenience. Ancient Rome featured indoor plumbing with aqueducts and pipes supplying homes and public fountains. Modern municipal water purification systems trace their origins to innovations like the Lyster Bag, developed for military use, and advancements in water treatment methods.
